pharm: Purified polyclonal human immunoglobulin G from pooled donor plasma that provides passive antibody (replacement) immunity and, at high doses, broad immunomodulation through Fc-receptor blockade, complement and autoantibody neutralization.
tags: BOXED WARNING - thrombosis and renal dysfunction (IVIG)
quick: Replacement IVIG ~300-600 mg/kg every 3-4 weeks; immunomodulatory (e.g., ITP) ~1 g/kg/day x1-2 or 0.4 g/kg/day x5
May be used when indicated; IgG crosses placenta; benefit usually outweighs risk
Caution - risk of acute renal failure (esp. sucrose-containing products); hydrate, slow infusion
Renal function, signs of thrombosis, hemolysis (Hb), infusion reactions, IgA status
summary: Human gamma globulin (immune globulin, IgG) is a sterile, purified preparation of polyclonal immunoglobulin G concentrated from large pools of human donor plasma. It is given intravenously (IVIG), subcutaneously (SCIG), or intramuscularly depending on the product and indication. As REPLACEMENT therapy it supplies protective antibody in primary and secondary humoral immunodeficiencies and provides passive prophylaxis against certain infections (e.g., hepatitis A, measles). At higher, IMMUNOMODULATORY doses it treats immune-mediated disorders such as immune thrombocytopenia, Kawasaki disease, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and others. Intravenous products carry a BOXED WARNING for thrombosis, acute renal dysfunction/failure (especially with sucrose-stabilized or high-osmolarity products and in patients with risk factors), and the possibility of acute renal failure; these risks are reduced by ensuring hydration, using the minimum infusion rate, and avoiding sucrose products in at-risk patients. Other notable reactions include infusion-related symptoms, aseptic meningitis, hemolysis, IgA-related hypersensitivity in IgA-deficient patients, and transfusion-related acute lung injury. This monograph is based on FDA prescribing information for human immune globulin products together with EMA sources.
indications: Replacement therapy for primary humoral immunodeficiency disorders
Secondary immunodeficiency (e.g., chronic lymphocytic leukemia, certain post-transplant or hypogammaglobulinemic states) with recurrent infection
Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura to raise platelet counts
Kawasaki disease (to reduce coronary artery aneurysms), Guillain-Barre syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy and multifocal motor neuropathy (product-specific)
Passive immunization/prophylaxis after exposure to certain infections (e.g., hepatitis A, measles) with intramuscular immune globulin

dosage.d: ~300-600 mg/kg every 3-4 weeks (titrate to trough IgG and clinical response)
dosage.n: Start at a low infusion rate and titrate up as tolerated

dosage.d: Weekly (or more frequent) subcutaneous dosing adjusted to maintain target IgG levels
dosage.n: Multiple infusion sites; steadier IgG levels, fewer systemic reactions

dosage.d: 1 g/kg/day for 1-2 days, or 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days
dosage.n: Watch for hemolysis and volume; titrate by platelet response

dosage.d: 2 g/kg as a single infusion (product-specific), usually with aspirin
dosage.n: Give early to reduce coronary aneurysm risk

dosage.d: Indication-specific (e.g., hepatitis A ~0.1-0.2 mL/kg; measles per weight)
dosage.n: Do not give IM products intravenously

admin: Ensure the patient is adequately hydrated before intravenous infusion; assess baseline renal function and thrombotic risk factors
Begin IV infusion at a slow initial rate and increase gradually as tolerated; slow or stop the infusion for adverse reactions
Use products without sucrose, and the lowest concentration and slowest practical rate, in patients at risk of renal failure or thrombosis
Determine IgA status when feasible - severe IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies raises anaphylaxis risk; use IgA-depleted products if needed
For subcutaneous administration, divide the dose across multiple sites; for intramuscular products, never give intravenously
Premedicate (antihistamine/antipyretic) per protocol if the patient has had prior infusion reactions, and keep epinephrine/resuscitation available
moa: Human gamma globulin provides intact polyclonal IgG antibodies. In replacement therapy it restores a broad repertoire of opsonizing and neutralizing antibodies against bacterial and viral antigens, providing passive humoral immunity to patients who cannot make adequate antibody. At high (immunomodulatory) doses its anti-inflammatory and immune-regulatory effects arise through several mechanisms: blockade of Fc receptors on macrophages (reducing destruction of antibody-coated cells, as in ITP), saturation/neutralization of pathogenic autoantibodies and complement components, modulation of cytokines and Fc-receptor expression, and effects on T- and B-cell function and the idiotype network. These combined actions dampen autoimmune and inflammatory tissue injury.

absolute: Severe IgA deficiency with documented antibodies against IgA and history of hypersensitivity (use IgA-depleted products with caution)
Known anaphylactic or severe systemic reaction to human immune globulin or components
Intramuscular products: do not administer intravenously; avoid IM in severe thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy
relative: Pre-existing renal impairment or risk factors for acute renal failure (diabetes, volume depletion, age >65, nephrotoxic drugs)
Thrombotic risk factors (prior thrombosis, immobilization, hyperviscosity, estrogen use, indwelling catheters)
Cardiac failure or states sensitive to volume load
monitor: Renal function (creatinine, urine output), especially with IVIG
Hemoglobin/hematocrit and signs of hemolysis (positive direct antiglobulin test)
Infusion reactions and vital signs during/after infusion
Trough IgG levels in replacement therapy

preg: Immune globulin (IgG) is given when clearly indicated in pregnancy; IgG crosses the placenta, particularly in the third trimester. Human experience suggests it can be used safely when the maternal benefit justifies treatment, and it is used for some pregnancy-related immune conditions.
lact: Immune globulin is considered compatible with breastfeeding; the antibodies may even confer passive immunity to the infant and there is no expected harm.
renal: Acute renal dysfunction and failure, osmotic nephrosis, and death have occurred with IVIG, most often with sucrose-stabilized or high-osmolar products and in patients with predisposing factors. Assess renal function before and periodically during therapy, ensure adequate hydration, use non-sucrose products at the minimum concentration and slowest rate in at-risk patients, and do not exceed recommended infusion rates.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment.

major: Live attenuated virus vaccines (measles, mumps, rubella, varicella) - passively acquired antibody can impair the immune response; defer such vaccination for an interval (commonly several months) after immune globulin
moderate: Other nephrotoxic drugs - additive risk of acute renal injury with IVIG
Drugs increasing thrombotic risk (e.g., estrogens) - additive thrombosis risk
minor: No significant pharmacokinetic drug interactions for the protein itself
interactions.diagnostics: Passively transferred antibodies can cause transient positive serologic tests and a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test; can cause false-positive blood-group antibody and infectious serology results; may transiently raise serum viscosity.

common: Local reactions at subcutaneous infusion sites
serious: Acute renal dysfunction/failure and osmotic nephrosis - BOXED WARNING (especially sucrose products)
rare: Transmission of blood-borne pathogens (very low risk with modern processing)
emergency: Acute thrombotic event (stroke, MI, DVT, PE)
Transfusion-related acute lung injury / acute respiratory distress

monitoring: Renal function (serum creatinine and urine output) before and during IVIG therapy
Vital signs and infusion reactions during and after each infusion
Hemoglobin/hematocrit and signs of hemolysis with high-dose therapy
Trough serum IgG levels and clinical infection control in replacement therapy
counsel: This is a blood-derived antibody product that boosts or modifies your immune system
Tell the staff immediately during the infusion if you feel chest tightness, breathlessness, severe headache, chills, or a rash
Drink plenty of fluids around the time of treatment, as advised, to protect your kidneys
Report leg swelling/pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke afterward - clots can occur
A severe headache with neck stiffness in the days after treatment can be a treatable inflammation of the lining of the brain - seek advice
Tell your doctor before having any live vaccines, which may need to be delayed for several months
pk: Immediate antibody availability after IV dosing; clinical immunomodulatory effect over hours to days
Peak serum IgG immediately after IV infusion; SC gives steadier, lower peaks
Protective antibody persists for weeks; replacement dosing every 3-4 weeks (IV) or weekly (SC)
Refrigerate (typically 2-8 C) per product; some products allow limited room-temperature storage; do not freeze; do not shake
pearls: This monograph is based on FDA prescribing information for human immune globulin products (a plasma-derived biologic) together with EMA sources

BOXED WARNING (IVIG): thrombosis and acute renal dysfunction/failure - ensure hydration, use the slowest rate/lowest concentration, avoid sucrose products in at-risk patients, and assess renal and thrombotic risk first
Two therapeutic modes: replacement (low dose, immunodeficiency) versus immunomodulation (high dose, e.g., ITP/Kawasaki/GBS/CIDP)
Severe IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies risks anaphylaxis - check IgA status and use IgA-depleted products
Delay live vaccines for several months after immune globulin (passive antibody blunts the response); expect a transient positive Coombs test
Watch for aseptic meningitis, hemolysis and TRALI; subcutaneous dosing gives steadier levels with fewer systemic reactions
missed: For scheduled replacement therapy, contact your clinic to reschedule a missed infusion as soon as possible to maintain protective antibody levels; do not attempt to make up doses on your own.
overdose: Overdose or rapid/large infusions may cause fluid overload and hyperviscosity, particularly in the elderly or those with cardiac or renal impairment, increasing the risk of thrombosis and renal injury. Management is supportive - slow or stop the infusion, monitor and support renal and cardiovascular function, maintain hydration, and watch for thrombotic complications.
